opus-5.5.text:
I think today's personal health monitoring is mostly about measurement without interpretation. You've got your Oura ring, your Apple Watch, maybe a continuous glucose monitor, and you get a lot of numbers. But the numbers don't really connect to anything actionable, and they definitely don't connect to the underlying biology of why you, specifically, are trending one way or another.

What I'd want from an AI doctor goes beyond a better dashboard. It would actually reason across all the layers of your data at once: your genome, your blood panels over time, your wearables, your family history, your medications, even things like single-cell or proteomic profiling as those get cheaper. And it should be able to say, "Here's what's changing, here's the most likely mechanism, here's what we'd expect to happen if you intervene this way versus that way." That's a predictive model of you, not a summary of you.

The second thing is continuity. Your human doctor sees you for fifteen minutes once a year and has to reconstruct your whole story from a chart. An AI doctor can hold your entire longitudinal history in context and notice the slow drifts that nobody catches, the kidney function that's been ticking down for five years, or the inflammatory marker that's subtly elevated every time something else happens. A lot of chronic disease is diagnosed far too late because no one is watching the trajectory.

The third thing, which I think is the most exciting, is closing the loop with experimentation. If you have a model that makes predictions about your biology, you can actually test them. Change something, measure, update. That turns medicine from a series of one-off guesses into something closer to a personalized scientific process, an n-of-1 trial running continuously.

And ultimately I'd want it to be connected to the frontier of biology, not just clinical guidelines that lag the research by a decade. If there's a new understanding of a disease mechanism or a new therapeutic, the AI doctor should be able to reason about whether it applies to you. That's where I think the real leap is: going from monitoring to actually understanding and predicting your biology, and helping you intervene earlier and more precisely than medicine can today.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes reasoning across multiple health data types, including genome, blood panels, wearables, family history, medications, and molecular profiling.

r002.rationale: The candidate says personal monitoring produces numbers that do not connect to actionable guidance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing to realize is that what we have today, even the best versions of it, is really just measurement. Your watch tells you your heart rate variability, your continuous glucose monitor tells you your glucose went up after lunch. It's descriptive. And what I actually want from an AI doctor is something that's not just descriptive but mechanistic and predictive, and ultimately interventional.

So let me break that down a little. The first thing is that most of the data we collect on ourselves is really low dimensional. A handful of biomarkers, some wearable signals. And the reason doctors are good is that they integrate across a huge amount of context, your history, your family, what you look like when you walk in the room, the thing you mentioned offhand. An AI doctor should be able to do that at a much higher resolution than any human can, across your genome, your proteome, your imaging, your longitudinal labs, and actually build a model of you as a person. Not a population average, but you.

The second thing is that once you have that model, you can start to reason about causality instead of correlation. Right now if your sleep score is bad, the app tells you it's bad. It doesn't tell you why, and it definitely doesn't tell you what will happen in five years if you don't change it. I want something that says, here's the trajectory you're on, here's the specific thing that's driving it, and here's the counterfactual if you intervene now.

And then the third piece, and this is the one I care about most coming from the biology side, is that the AI doctor should close the loop. It shouldn't just recommend, it should be connected to the design of the intervention itself. Because for a lot of disease, especially rare disease, the right drug doesn't exist yet. So the real version of this is an AI doctor that can look at a patient, figure out the mechanism, and then actually help design the therapy, whether that's a small molecule or a gene editing approach or something else. That's when it stops being monitoring and starts being medicine.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI doctor should integrate genome, proteome, imaging, longitudinal labs, wearable signals, and personal history into a model of the individual.

r002.rationale: The response says monitoring is descriptive and does not explain why a measure is bad or predict what may happen, but it does not clearly state that descriptive monitoring alone fails to tell the person what health actions to take.

astra-6.text:
I’d want an AI doctor to go beyond telling me what’s happening and help me understand what to do about it. A wearable might tell you that you slept poorly or that your resting heart rate is elevated. The more useful question is: Why? Is this a normal fluctuation, something about your behavior, or something that warrants a closer look?

That requires understanding you over time—your medical history, your baseline, your environment—and knowing when to ask more questions, recommend a test, or bring in a human physician. It should also be able to say, “We don’t have enough information yet.”

Ultimately, I’d want that kind of careful, personalized care to be available to everyone. Something that helps you stay healthy and navigate decisions, rather than just giving you another dashboard of numbers to worry about.

r001.rationale: It mentions a wearable, medical history, baseline, and environment, but does not clearly propose integrating multiple health data modalities.

r002.rationale: It contrasts reporting signals such as poor sleep or elevated heart rate with helping the person understand what to do about them.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want them to move from monitoring to actually helping you make decisions. A wearable can tell you that your sleep was poor or your heart rate is elevated, but what does that mean for you, and what should you do next? An AI doctor should be able to put those signals in context with your medical history, medications, and what’s happening in your life, then help you figure out whether something needs attention.

And ideally, that becomes a continuous relationship. You shouldn’t have to reconstruct your entire health history in a fifteen-minute appointment. The system should help you understand your options, recognize when it’s uncertain, and bring in a human clinician when that’s needed. The goal is better health and more agency over your health, rather than just more data.

r001.rationale: It proposes putting wearable signals such as sleep and heart rate in context with medical history, medications, and life circumstances.

r002.rationale: It says monitoring can report poor sleep or elevated heart rate but does not explain what they mean or what action to take.
